guidance.opening:
It is autumn 1920 in Boston. You are in a landlord's small office because he sent for someone willing to look into a house that will not stay rented. The window is open a crack, and the street noise comes in with the dust.

"Sit down. I'm Steven Knott. I inherited a place no one will keep. Last family packed up after a bad scare—some of them ended up in a sanitarium—and now the neighbors talk, and I can't let it. I need a pair of eyes who can find out what's wrong and get the house a decent name again. We'll talk money later; I just want to know who I'm looking at."

He taps a pencil against the blotter, waiting. "So—who are you, and what do you do for a living? A rough answer will do."
guidance.advice: Use only listed occupation names. For 1920s Boston public hire by a landlord: Journalist, Private Investigator, Lawyer, Librarian, Police Detective, Police Officer, Professor, Author, Antiquarian, Parapsychologist, Doctor of Medicine, Engineer, Dilettante, Clergy, and Criminal (as a discreet fixer) fit the public premise of looking into a house and paper trails. Useful training: Library Use, History, Law, Persuade, Fast Talk, Spot Hidden, Listen, Psychology, Occult as rumor-chasing not confirmed fact, Locksmith only if the player chooses a burglar-adjacent Criminal. Languages: English is assumed; Latin or Italian can be optional flavor for records or last tenants, never required. Belongings: notebook, press card, letter of introduction, modest 1920s street clothes, flashlight—no house keys or advance pay yet. Public involvement: hired-by-the-day prospect, not yet commissioned. Optional ties (not facts): a cousin who once rented in that neighborhood, a paper that killed a story, a sanitarium acquaintance. Do not invent numbers or force a profession. Authored constraint: identity meeting only; no keys, cash, address, or accepted job.
guidance.handoff: The visitor has met landlord Steven Knott in his Boston office in autumn 1920. Knott has explained, in public terms only, that an inherited house will not stay rented after the last family fled in fright, and that he wants someone to look into what is wrong and restore the property's reputation. He has asked who the visitor is and what they do. No commission has been accepted, and no keys, cash, address, or other items have been given. Continue from this identity conversation in Knott's Office.
